Paper_name: Can irrelevant self-related information in working memory be actively suppressed?
Summary: This study examined whether task-irrelevant identity-associated information (self, friend, stranger) can be actively suppressed in working memory, using an irrelevant-distracting paradigm in which participants memorized colors while ignoring shapes during a memory array, then judged whether the test color matched the memorized one while the ignored shape features could also change. Both experiments consisted of two stages: a training phase (shape-label associative-learning task, i.e. the matching task stored in this database) followed by a test phase (irrelevant distracting task). In Experiment 1 (46 participants tested, 42 analyzed; labels self/friend/stranger), self-associated information survived the inhibitory effect. In Experiment 2 (38 tested, 36 analyzed; labels self/stranger plus two neutral shapes, ISI manipulated at 1000 vs 3000 ms), stranger-associated information showed an inhibitory effect at the long ISI while self-associated information remained uninhibited regardless of ISI. The associative-learning task confirmed the self-advantage in both experiments (self faster and more accurate than other identities).
Author: Quan Zhang, Tiangang Zhou, Jin Tang, Huanjun Xi
Conclusion: Self-associated information can bypass the executive system and remain active in working memory processing: attended but outdated self-related features cannot be inhibited, whereas stranger-associated features were suppressed at a long maintenance interval (3000 ms) in Experiment 2.
